bibl.title: Advancing mathematics by guiding human intuition with AI

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: The conjecture-making stage of mathematical practice, and whether a supervised model plus attribution can guide it.
span.quote: One of the central drivers of mathematical progress is the discovery of patterns and formulation of useful conjectures: statements that are suspected to be true but have not been proven to hold in all cases.

span.label: Computers have generated mathematical data for decades - can a learned model do the harder thing and help a mathematician see which relationships are worth conjecturing?
span.quote: Prior systems for generating conjectures have either contributed genuinely useful research conjectures 9 via methods that do not easily generalize to other mathematical areas 10 , or have demonstrated novel, general methods for finding conjectures 11 that have not yet yielded mathematically valuable results.

span.label: A framework - hypothesise a relation, learn it, attribute it, conjecture a closed form - demonstrated by two genuinely new results in different areas of pure mathematics.
span.quote: Our contribution shows how mature machine learning methodologies can be adapted and integrated into existing mathematical workflows to achieve novel results.

span.label: method
span.quote: We propose a process of using machine learning to discover potential patterns and relations between mathematical objects, understanding them with attribution techniques and using these observations to guide intuition and propose conjectures.

span.label: machine-learning-guided mathematical conjecture discovery
span.quote: One of the central drivers of mathematical progress is the discovery of patterns and formulation of useful conjectures: statements that are suspected to be true but have not been proven to hold in all cases.

span.label: system-or-tool-building
span.quote: We propose a framework for augmenting the standard mathematician’s toolkit with powerful pattern recognition and interpretation methods from machine learning and demonstrate its value and generality by showing how it led us to two fundamental new discoveries, one in topology and another in representation theory.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Supervised learning first certifies that a pattern exists at all (better-than-chance prediction), then attribution techniques localise which input features carry it, so the mathematician's search space is narrowed before any conjecture is formed
span.quote: The framework helps guide the intuition of mathematicians in two ways: by verifying the hypothesized existence of structure/patterns in mathematical objects through the use of supervised machine learning; and by helping in the understanding of these patterns through the use of attribution techniques.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Gradient saliency assigns importance by measuring how much the learned function's prediction shifts under small perturbations of each input component
span.quote: These techniques attribute importance to the elements of X ( z ), by calculating how much f ˆ changes in predictions of Y (z) given small changes in X ( z ).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: accuracy above chance is used as evidence that a relationship EXISTS, before anyone knows what it is - the model detects presence, not content
span.quote: If f ˆ is more accurate than would be expected by chance, it indicates that there may be such a relationship to explore.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: attribution turns an opaque learned function into something a person can reason about, by showing which inputs it is sensitive to
span.quote: Attribution techniques can be used to understand which aspects of f ˆ are relevant for predictions of Y ( z ).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the human keeps the selection step: conjectures are chosen for being interesting and suggestive of a proof, not merely for fitting
span.quote: In this process, the mathematician can guide the choice of conjectures to those that not just fit the data but also seem interesting, plausibly true and, ideally, suggestive of a proof strategy.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the loop is iterative rather than a pipeline - the framework expects several passes before a conjecture is worth stating
span.quote: This iterative process might need to be repeated several times before a viable conjecture is settled on.

span.label: The framework needs large generatable datasets and patterns visible in computable examples
span.quote: There are limitations to where this framework will be useful—it requires the ability to generate large datasets of the representations of objects and for the patterns to be detectable in examples that are calculable.

span.label: In some domains the target functions may simply not be learnable this way
span.quote: Further, in some domains the functions of interest may be difficult to learn in this paradigm.

span.label: Conclusions hold only for the sampling distribution used, not the whole space
span.quote: The results of the subsequent stages will hold true only for the distribution P Z , and not the whole space Z .

span.label: A negative result is uninformative: failure to predict does not mean no pattern exists
span.quote: The converse is not true; namely, if the model cannot predict the relationship better than chance, it may mean that a pattern exists, but is sufficiently complicated that it cannot be captured by the given model and training procedure.

span.label: Two demonstrations in two areas; the generality of the framework is argued from them rather than established.
span.quote: We propose a framework for augmenting the standard mathematician’s toolkit with powerful pattern recognition and interpretation methods from machine learning and demonstrate its value and generality by showing how it led us to two fundamental new discoveries, one in topology and another in representation theory.

span.label: The paper is explicit that the older data-driven route fails as objects get higher-dimensional or more structured - which is the regime the framework is for, and also the regime where its own outputs are hardest to check.
span.quote: However, for X ( z ) and Y ( z ) in higher-dimensional spaces, or of more complex types, such as graphs, and for more complicated, nonlinear f ˆ , this approach is either less useful or entirely infeasible.

span.label: Every step that decides whether a pattern is worth pursuing is human; the framework does not claim to automate judgement.
span.quote: In this process, the mathematician can guide the choice of conjectures to those that not just fit the data but also seem interesting, plausibly true and, ideally, suggestive of a proof strategy.

span.label: pattern-recognition and model-interpretation methods are imported wholesale into the working practice of pure mathematics, as an addition to the mathematician's toolkit
span.quote: We propose a framework for augmenting the standard mathematician’s toolkit with powerful pattern recognition and interpretation methods from machine learning and demonstrate its value and generality by showing how it led us to two fundamental new discoveries, one in topology and another in representation theory.

span.label: the gradient-based attribution method used to interpret the trained network is identified as the machine-learning counterpart of sensitivity analysis
span.quote: In this work we use gradient-based techniques 40 , broadly similar to sensitivity analysis in classical statistics and sometimes referred to as saliency maps.

span.label: supervised regression and gradient-based attribution, imported into pure mathematics not to prove anything but to indicate where a relationship might exist
span.quote: Our contribution shows how mature machine learning methodologies can be adapted and integrated into existing mathematical workflows to achieve novel results.

span.label: intuition - as the faculty being ASSISTED: a hypothesis the mathematician brings, which the model then confirms or fails to confirm
span.quote: In the supervised learning stage, the mathematician proposes a hypothesis that there exists a relationship between X ( z ) and Y ( z ).

span.label: intuition - as the faculty being TESTED: the framework as a bench on which a hunch can be checked cheaply before it is pursued
span.quote: Conceptually, this framework provides a ‘test bed for intuition’—quickly verifying whether an intuition about the relationship between two quantities may be worth pursuing and, if so, guidance as to how they may be related.

span.label: discovery - as detecting that a relation exists, which the model does
span.quote: If f ˆ is more accurate than would be expected by chance, it indicates that there may be such a relationship to explore.

span.label: discovery - as deciding which relation is worth stating, which stays with the mathematician
span.quote: In this process, the mathematician can guide the choice of conjectures to those that not just fit the data but also seem interesting, plausibly true and, ideally, suggestive of a proof strategy.

span.label: extends → prior work using supervised learning to find patterns in mathematics (the paper's refs 20-24)
span.quote: This extends work using supervised learning to find patterns 20 – 24 by focusing on enabling mathematicians to understand the learned functions and derive useful mathematical insight.

span.label: extends → the combinatorial invariance conjecture for symmetric groups
span.quote: This conjectured solution, if proven true, would settle the combinatorial invariance conjecture for symmetric groups.

span.label: builds-on → prior work on subgraphs of Bruhat intervals (the paper's ref 31)
span.quote: In particular, we found that a subgraph inspired by prior work 31 may be sufficient to calculate the KL polynomial, and this was supported by a much more accurate estimated function.

span.label: extends → prior supervised-learning work on finding patterns in mathematical data
span.quote: This extends work using supervised learning to find patterns 20 – 24 by focusing on enabling mathematicians to understand the learned functions and derive useful mathematical insight.

span.label: builds-on → the long tradition of computer-generated data in conjecture formation, from Gauss's prime tables to Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer
span.quote: Mathematicians have always used data to help in this process—from the early hand-calculated prime tables used by Gauss and others that led to the prime number theorem 5 , to modern computer-generated data 1 , 5 in cases such as the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture 2 .

span.label: contradicts → prior conjecture-generation systems, as either non-generalisable or not yet mathematically useful
span.quote: Prior systems for generating conjectures have either contributed genuinely useful research conjectures 9 via methods that do not easily generalize to other mathematical areas 10 , or have demonstrated novel, general methods for finding conjectures 11 that have not yet yielded mathematically valuable results.

span.label: gradient saliency —is-a→ attribution techniques
span.quote: The attribution technique we use in our work, gradient saliency, does this by calculating the derivative of outputs of f ˆ , with respect to the inputs.

span.label: supervised learning —part-of→ machine learning
span.quote: The key contributions of machine learning in this regression process are the broad set of possible nonlinear functions that can be learned given a sufficient amount of data.

span.label: machine learning —causes→ intuition
span.quote: We propose a process of using machine learning to discover potential patterns and relations between mathematical objects, understanding them with attribution techniques and using these observations to guide intuition and propose conjectures.

span.label: intuition —causes→ conjecture
span.quote: In this process, the mathematician can guide the choice of conjectures to those that not just fit the data but also seem interesting, plausibly true and, ideally, suggestive of a proof strategy.

span.label: classification accuracy
span.quote: The task was framed as a multi-class classification problem, with the distinct values of the signature as classes, cross-entropy loss as an optimizable loss function and test classification accuracy as a metric of performance.

span.label: confidence interval
span.quote: The 95% confidence interval error bars are across 10 retrainings of the model.

span.label: bootstrap
span.quote: The percentage of observed edges of each type in the salient subgraph for 10 retrainings of the model compared to 10 bootstrapped samples of the same size from the dataset.

span.label: train/test split (held-out evaluation)
span.quote: We split the intervals randomly into train/test partitions at 80%/20%.

span.label: standardization (mean and variance)
span.quote: All features are normalized by subtracting the mean and dividing by the variance.

span.label: regression
span.quote: The key contributions of machine learning in this regression process are the broad set of possible nonlinear functions that can be learned given a sufficient amount of data.

span.label: accuracy
span.quote: If f ˆ is more accurate than would be expected by chance, it indicates that there may be such a relationship to explore.

span.label: The proposed machine-learning framework produced genuinely new mathematics in two unrelated fields: a knot-theoretic connection between algebraic and geometric invariants, and a candidate resolution of a long-open conjecture in representation theory.
span.quote: In this work we have demonstrated a framework for mathematicians to use machine learning that has led to mathematical insight across two distinct disciplines: one of the first connections between the algebraic and geometric structure of knots and a proposed resolution to a long-standing open conjecture in representation theory.

span.label: A feed-forward network predicted knot signature from geometric invariants far better than chance, which was taken as evidence that a real relationship exists.
span.quote: The model was able to achieve an accuracy of 78% on a held-out test set, with no errors larger than ±2.

span.label: Attribution pointed to the cusp shape, and the derived 'natural slope' turned out to capture linearly all the information about the signature that the full geometric model had extracted.
span.quote: This implies that the slope linearly captures all of the information about the signature that the original model had extracted from the geometry.

span.label: The resulting theorem is among the first to link algebraic and geometric knot invariants and has further consequences for Dehn surgeries and surface genus.
span.quote: The above theorem is one of the first results that connect the algebraic and geometric invariants of knots and has various interesting applications.

span.label: The first conjectured inequality, though supported by large sampled datasets, was false: specially constructed braids furnished counterexamples and forced a corrected theorem.
span.quote: While this conjecture was supported by an analysis of several large datasets sampled from different distributions, we were able to construct counterexamples using braids of a specific form.

span.label: Salient-subgraph analysis in the representation-theory case led to the discovery that a Bruhat interval decomposes into a hypercube plus a graph isomorphic to an interval in the smaller symmetric group.
span.quote: Considering this observation led us to the discovery that there is a natural decomposition of an interval into two parts—a hypercube induced by one set of extremal edges and a graph isomorphic to an interval in S N −1 .

span.label: This decomposition yields a proved theorem: every Bruhat interval admits a canonical hypercube decomposition from which the Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomial can be computed directly.
span.quote: Every Bruhat interval admits a canonical hypercube decomposition along its extremal reflections, from which the KL polynomial is directly computable.

span.label: Computational testing suggested the stronger claim that any hypercube decomposition, not just the canonical one, recovers the correct KL polynomial.
span.quote: Remarkably, further tests suggested that all hypercube decompositions correctly determine the KL polynomial.

span.label: Edge labels absent from the input were nonetheless reflected in the network's saliency pattern, since extremal reflections were overrepresented in salient subgraphs.
span.quote: This is notable because the edge labels are not given to the network and are not recoverable from the unlabelled Bruhat interval.

span.label: The framework produced two genuinely new mathematical results - a connection between algebraic and geometric invariants of knots, and a candidate algorithm for the combinatorial invariance conjecture.
span.quote: Here we provide examples of new fundamental results in pure mathematics that have been discovered with the assistance of machine learning—demonstrating a method by which machine learning can aid mathematicians in discovering new conjectures and theorems.

span.label: Earlier conjecture-generating systems split into two failure modes: useful but not generalisable, or general but not yet useful.
span.quote: Prior systems for generating conjectures have either contributed genuinely useful research conjectures 9 via methods that do not easily generalize to other mathematical areas 10 , or have demonstrated novel, general methods for finding conjectures 11 that have not yet yielded mathematically valuable results.

span.label: The computational cost is small - hours on a single GPU - so the constraint is mathematical judgement, not compute.
span.quote: In each of these cases, the necessary models can be trained within several hours on a machine with a single graphics processing unit.

span.label: AI had already been used in mathematics for counterexamples, calculation and symbolic solutions; what was missing was help with discovery itself.
span.quote: In mathematics, it has been shown that AI can be used as a valuable tool by finding counterexamples to existing conjectures 16 , accelerating calculations 17 , generating symbolic solutions 18 and detecting the existence of structure in mathematical objects 19 .
